articles.title: Is Claude Nerfed? Build a 20-Task Eval Canary in an Afternoon
articles.excerpt: "Is Claude nerfed" is unanswerable from vibes, and a 20-task nightly canary that costs about $27.60 a month on Sonnet 5.5, or $1.38 on Haiku 5.5, answers it with numbers. The Hacker News thread "Liven…
articles.body: "Is Claude nerfed" is unanswerable from vibes, and a 20-task nightly canary that costs about $27.60 a month on Sonnet 5.5, or $1.38 on Haiku 5.5, answers it with numbers. The Hacker News thread "Livenerf: Has Opus 5.5 been nerfed yet?" reached 924 points and 394 comments ( item 49901736 ), and the loudest voices on both sides had no baseline. This post builds one: 20 fixed tasks, a pinned model and effort level, graders that run code instead of reading tone, a drift threshold, and a GitHub Action that runs it at 02:17 UTC every night. Then it shows how to tell a real regression from drift you caused yourself. Why "it feels dumber" can't be tested Every complaint in that thread is a comparison against a memory.

articles.title: LINE Has No Web Version: How to Translate LINE Chats on a Desktop
articles.excerpt: Disclosure: I work on Liao, which is one of the options below. Many people who work with customers in Japan, Thailand and Taiwan end up chatting on LINE. There is one problem: unlike WhatsApp or Teleg…
articles.body: Disclosure: I work on Liao, which is one of the options below. Many people who work with customers in Japan, Thailand and Taiwan end up chatting on LINE. There is one problem: unlike WhatsApp or Telegram, LINE has no web version . It offers a phone app, a desktop client and a browser extension. That is why the "translate in the browser" tricks that work on other chat apps do not work here. What people usually do Copy and paste into a translation app. It needs no setup, but every message means switching windows, and replying takes a second round trip. A translation bot in the chat. You add a bot as a friend or invite it into a group, and it posts translations. It works well in group chats.

articles.title: Google Play holds my app hostage until 12 strangers use it for 14 days. So I'm building the swap club.
articles.excerpt: 🇧🇷 Versão em português nos comentários (vou postar o link assim que sair). Personal Google Play accounts created after Nov 13, 2023 cannot publish to production until they run a closed test with a m…
articles.body: 🇧🇷 Versão em português nos comentários (vou postar o link assim que sair). The wall Personal Google Play accounts created after Nov 13, 2023 cannot publish to production until they run a closed test with a minimum of 12 testers for 14 consecutive days . Think about what that means if you're solo: You built an app. Alone. Now Google requires you to know 12 actual humans who will install it, keep it installed, and use it, for two weeks straight. Your mom counts as 1. Your secondary email doesn't count. Your dog doesn't have a Google account. Every solo dev without a network stalls here. Paid services emerged charging $15–25 per app to supply the testers. Swap groups on Reddit/Telegram exist... and most die by day 3 because nobody tracks anything and everyone starts on a different day.

articles.excerpt: Our monitoring dashboard insisted that everything was fine. Across an entire week and every single namespace in a production Kubernetes platform, we recorded exactly eight container restarts. Meanwhil…
articles.body: Our monitoring dashboard insisted that everything was fine. Across an entire week and every single namespace in a production Kubernetes platform, we recorded exactly eight container restarts. Meanwhile, customer reports kept piling in: live calls were abruptly cutting off. Both statements were completely accurate. The dashboard was simply answering a different question from the one our users were experiencing. Bridging that disconnect required chaining four specialized AI assistants, asking precise forensic questions, and sticking to one non-negotiable rule: nothing an assistant says counts as evidence until it is backed by an executable query, a raw log line, or a verifiable platform event.

articles.title: Hash Three Boundaries Before You Blame the Model
articles.excerpt: A night operator opened two logs for the same tool call. The process log held valid JSON with two rows. The next model turn claimed the tool result was unreadable. This scene is reconstructed for teac…
articles.body: A night operator opened two logs for the same tool call. The process log held valid JSON with two rows. The next model turn claimed the tool result was unreadable. This scene is reconstructed for teaching, not a quoted outage. The figures below are fixtures, not measured production rates. The handoff has three owners A tool process writes the first byte string. An adapter then parses, wraps, or redacts that string. A prompt builder copies one slice into the next model message. Any owner can change bytes without changing the tool name. A single stored hash cannot say which owner did it. You need one digest per boundary, plus the length at that boundary. Fields worth storing Keep these fields on the same tool-call row. Derive mutation_hop in code, not in an editor.

articles.title: Langflow never asked you for a password? Check LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN in one request
articles.excerpt: If you installed Langflow with pip or uv and ran langflow run, it never asked you to sign in. That isn't a missing feature. It's auto-login, and Langflow's docs describe it plainly: it "automatically…
articles.body: If you installed Langflow with pip or uv and ran langflow run , it never asked you to sign in. That isn't a missing feature. It's auto-login , and Langflow's docs describe it plainly: it "automatically signs in all users as the configured superuser". LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN defaults to True for pip installs. The docs add that "official Langflow Docker images set false ", so the same app behaves differently depending on how you installed it. On a laptop nobody else can reach, that's fine. On a server, a shared machine or a forwarded port, anyone who can open the page is the admin. In Langflow, the admin can edit a component's Python code, and that code runs on your host. Check it in one request When the editor loads, it calls /api/v1/auto_login .

articles.title: How to stop one customer from blowing up your OpenAI bill
articles.excerpt: If you run a SaaS on top of an LLM API, your provider bill is one number. OpenAI and Anthropic let you set limits per organization or project. Those limits protect your account, not your margins: they…
articles.body: If you run a SaaS on top of an LLM API, your provider bill is one number. OpenAI and Anthropic let you set limits per organization or project. Those limits protect your account, not your margins: they can't tell you which customer drove the spend, and they can't stop one customer without stopping everyone. There are two ways this goes wrong: The runaway user. Someone scripts your feature, or a client bug retries in a loop, and one account burns real money overnight. The quietly unprofitable account. A customer on a $20 plan sends long contexts every day and costs you more in tokens than they pay. You can't see it because cost isn't attributed per customer. Here's a pattern that fixes both, and the edge cases to watch for. 1.

articles.excerpt: NASA is asking for ideas to stop static electricity from zapping astronauts or critical hardware during moon missions.
articles.body: NASA is asking for ideas to stop static electricity from zapping astronauts or critical hardware during moon missions. The agency opened a "Lunar Grounding Challenge" to avoid situations where an astronaut on the moon could become "a walking, high voltage capacitor." Submissions for the $150,000 competition are due Jan. 15 and you can see the requirements here . NASA is hoping to put astronaut boots at the lunar south pole in 2028 during the Artemis 4 or 5 missions, on the first landing mission since NASA's Apollo 17 in 1972. articles.title: The 'Halloween Fireballs' are coming. Here's what to expect from the Taurids this year
articles.excerpt: The Southern and Northern Taurid meteor showers will produce occasional bright, slow-moving meteors worldwide during October and November, with moon-free peaks in 2026.
articles.body: They don't produce anything like the torrent of "shooting stars" associated with August's Perseids or December's Geminids, but the Taurid meteor showers have something else going for them — fireballs. The Taurids are famous for occasionally producing exceptionally bright, slow-moving meteors that can streak dramatically across the night sky from September to December. As a bonus, they're visible from both the Northern and Southern hemispheres. That's because they appear to emanate from the constellation Taurus, which sits close to the ecliptic, the apparent path the sun takes across the sky as Earth orbits around it. The Taurids are actually two closely related showers — the Southern Taurids and Northern Taurids — whose activity overlaps in late October and November.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 12, 1964: The Soviet Union launches Voskhod 1, the 1st multi-person cosmonaut crew, into space
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight . This was the first time that a spacecraft carried more than one person into orbit, with three cosmonauts packed inside the spacecraft. Only two cosmonauts were originally supposed to fly on this mission, but Soviet politicians pressured the Russian space program to add one more. This left no room for spacesuits on board, so this also became the first spaceflight without spacesuits . Two of the crewmembers, an engineer and a doctor, became the first civilians to go to space. On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched the first multiperson mission, Voskhod 1, which launched three Russian cosmonauts into space.

articles.title: Namibian salt flats look like an alien planet | Space photo of the day for Oct. 12, 2026
articles.excerpt: The Etosha Pan in northern Namibia, the largest salt flat in the country, looks otherworldly in this satellite photo.
articles.body: The Etosha Pan, Namibia's largest salt pan, seen from space. (Image credit: Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2026), processed by ESA) A neon blue pool swirls amongst what look like clouds, all surrounded by a bright red stretch of land. This might look like the surface of an alien planet , but it's actually a salt flat right here on Earth , seen from space. What is it? Etosha National Park in northern Namibia hosts the largest salt pan, or piece of land covered with salt and other minerals, in the country. This image of the Etosha Pan was captured on April 5 of this year by Europe's Copernicus Sentinel-2 mission, which consists of two identical satellites in the same orbit.
